topicName: Water and inorganic ions in plants

cards.front: What is turgor pressure in a plant cell?
cards.back: **Turgor pressure** is the pressure the cell contents exert on the cell wall when the vacuole is full of water. The wall resists stretching, so it pushes back and keeps the cell firm.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to the vacuole when water enters by osmosis.

cards.front: Why does a non-woody plant like lettuce stay upright?
cards.back: Many **turgid** cells press against their walls, so soft stems stay supported and leaves are held out to catch light.
cards.hint: Think about what turgid cells do together, not on their own.

cards.front: What does each of the three main inorganic ions help a plant to make?
cards.back: **Nitrate** supplies nitrogen for amino acids, proteins and nucleotides. **Magnesium** forms part of every chlorophyll molecule. **Calcium** forms calcium pectate, which joins neighbouring cell walls.
cards.hint: Name the ion first, then the molecule it helps to build.

cards.back: **Transpiration** is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. It also pulls more water and dissolved ions up from the roots through the xylem.
cards.hint: Think about where most water leaves a plant.

cards.back: **Plasmolysis** is the shrinking of the cytoplasm and membrane away from the cell wall after water is lost by osmosis, usually in a strongly concentrated solution.
cards.hint: Compare it with what happens to turgor pressure when water is lost.

cards.front: Why does a plant wilt when the soil dries out?
cards.back: Water leaves the cells by osmosis, so the vacuole shrinks and turgor pressure falls. The cell becomes **flaccid**, and the whole plant wilts.
cards.hint: Follow the vacuole as the soil loses its water.

cards.front: What happens to a plant cell placed in pure water, and why?
cards.back: It becomes turgid rather than bursting, because the cell wall resists stretching. Bursting would only happen if the wall could not hold the pressure.
cards.hint: Think about how strong the cell wall is compared with a balloon.

cards.back: **Chlorosis** is the yellowing of normally green plant tissue, caused by too little chlorophyll.
cards.hint: Think about what chlorophyll gives leaves their colour.

cards.front: Why does chlorosis alone not tell you which ion is missing?
cards.back: Nitrate and magnesium shortages can both cause yellowing. You need the pattern of symptoms, such as which leaves are affected, to identify the ion.
cards.hint: Consider which other ions could cause the same colour change.

cards.front: Why do older leaves show nitrate or magnesium shortage first?
cards.back: Both ions can be moved out of old leaves through the phloem to growing tips. Calcium moves poorly, so young tissues suffer first when it runs short.
cards.hint: Think about how the plant moves useful ions around its body.

cards.front: What are the steps of a culture solution experiment to find which ion a plant needs?
cards.back: Make a complete control solution and others each lacking one ion. Grow identical seedlings in each, keep light, temperature and volume the same, aerate the roots, then measure growth over several weeks.
cards.hint: Start with the control, then think about what you change.

cards.front: Why is dry mass the most reliable growth measure in a culture solution experiment?
cards.back: Water content varies between plants, so it can mislead. Dry mass removes this variation, and you should use several plants per solution and calculate means.
cards.hint: Think about how much water a plant can hold.

cards.front: What are water's roles as a reactant in plants?
cards.back: Water is split in photosynthesis and used in hydrolysis, so it is a **reactant** as well as a solvent and coolant.
cards.hint: Think about which processes in the plant break molecules apart.
